stem: A prompt asks a chat model for the total cost of a shipment after weight tiers, a fuel surcharge and a discount. Asked for the number directly, the model often returns a wrong total, although each single rule is applied correctly when asked alone. Which prompt change most directly helps?

Tell the model that its answer is very important and that it must not make any mistakes in the total
Ask the model to work through each rule step by step and then give the final total on a last line
Move the pricing rules to the end of the prompt, since the last instruction is always the one followed

stem: A developer sends a `json_schema` `response_format` to a Foundation Model APIs chat endpoint. In the schema the `currency` property has a regex `pattern` and `price` uses `anyOf` to accept either a string or a number. The request is rejected or the constraints are not applied, and the team still needs schema-conforming JSON. What should the developer do?

choices.text: Use plain `string` and `number` properties, list the allowed currency codes in the field description, and validate in code
Keep the schema and switch `type` to `json_object`, which applies the schema's regular expression during decoding
Declare `price` as `"type": ["string", "number"]`, since a list of types replaces `anyOf` in this subset

stem: A prompt asks a chat model to label support tickets as `billing`, `outage` or `other`. Replies vary between "Billing", "This looks like a billing issue" and "billing." Which TWO changes most directly make the output a single, stable label? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Raise the temperature to 2 so the model explores more phrasings and settles on one

Add "be creative with the label wording" to the system message to prompt a consistent style
Increase `max_tokens` so that the model has enough room to finish its explanation before the label
Include two or three example tickets in the prompt, each followed by exactly the label text the application expects

stem: A support assistant must always answer in Korean, in at most three bullet points, and never speculate beyond the supplied context. Each turn carries a new user question and new retrieved passages. Where should these standing rules live in the chat request?

In a one-time setup request per session, because the endpoint stores them for later calls
In an assistant message placed before the first user turn so the model treats them as its own earlier output
In the system message, with only the question and passages sent in each user message

stem: A tool lets analysts paste any text and name whichever fields they want extracted (for example "supplier, due date" one day and "diagnosis, dosage" the next). The field list is not known at development time, but the reply must always be valid JSON. Which `response_format` fits?

choices.text: A `json_schema` using `anyOf` so that each analyst's field list becomes its own branch
`{"type": "json_object"}` with the requested field names given in the prompt
Plain text, then a regular expression in application code that pulls the key-value pairs
A `json_schema` that lists every field name any analyst might ask for, all marked optional

stem: A team uses a `json_schema` response format with five fields and `max_tokens=64`. Short documents give correct objects, but for long documents the JSON stops in the middle of a string and fails to parse. What is the fix?

Raise the temperature so the model produces a more compact object for long documents
Add a stop sequence at the closing brace so the model ends the object itself
Remove `response_format` so the model is free to shorten its output

stem: A helpdesk wants to show agents the five past tickets that are closest in meaning to a new ticket, even when no keywords match. Which model task should the application use?

A classification model that assigns every ticket one of a fixed set of categories and matches on the category
An embedding model that turns tickets and the new ticket into vectors, ranked by similarity
A summarization function that shortens each ticket, followed by a keyword match on the summaries

stem: Analysts must assign each of three million rows in a Unity Catalog table to one of six topic labels using SQL. They have no prompt-engineering experience and want the least setup. Which option fits best?

`ai_query` with a hand-written prompt and a custom parser for each model reply

stem: A RAG chain must return its answer together with the source of each passage it used. Which TWO changes support this? (Select TWO)

stem: Sales reps lose hours searching past RFP answers. The team wants a GenAI assistant that cuts that time. Which input/output description is the best translation of this goal for the pipeline?

stem: A multinational's support assistant must answer from knowledge-base articles, but agents may only see articles for their own region. Which description of the pipeline input and behavior meets the requirement?

Agent Runtime with AgentKit, which hosts any framework and adds durable execution that survives restarts
MLflow Tracing, which records every step of a run and automatically replays the failed step after the host comes back

stem: Finance analysts want a business-user assistant that answers natural-language questions about governed sales tables. The data team wants to configure trusted data, metrics and business rules and does not want to write agent code. Which option fits best?

An agent scaffolded with the Agent Bricks CLI, with SQL generation written by the team in Python

stem: A contract-search RAG index was built by cutting every document into 800-character pieces with a fixed-size splitter. Retrieved chunks often start in the middle of a sentence and end in the middle of the next clause, and answers cite half a clause. What is the best change to the chunking step?

Raise the chunk size to the whole document so that no clause is ever cut
Switch to a recursive splitter that prefers paragraph and sentence boundaries before it cuts by length
Keep the 800-character pieces but remove every period so that sentences cannot be split

Cut each chunk to a single sentence so that any exception becomes its own chunk
Remove the overlap and rely on a deduplication job to repair the cuts afterwards

Treat each table element apart from prose, split only between rows, and repeat the header in every piece

Store the heading path and a short document summary as metadata columns next to the chunk, and return them with it (a reranker can also read them)

stem: Support answers often depend on a single sentence inside a long troubleshooting article, but the sentences before and after it explain the exception. The team wants to retrieve with very precise embeddings and still give the model the neighboring text. Which approach matches this goal?

choices.text: Sentence-window retrieval: embed single sentences and return each hit with a fixed number of sentences on each side
Fixed-size chunking at 2,000 characters with no overlap, so that each chunk is large enough to hold the sentence and its neighbors
Summarize each article and embed only the summary, so that the retriever returns one short abstract for every article it matches
Keyword-only retrieval on the article title, so that the full article is returned whenever any title term matches the question

stem: A legal team is choosing between recursive character splitting and semantic chunking (splitting where the topic changes, based on embedding similarity between adjacent sentences) for 4 million pages that must be re-chunked each time the policy changes. Which statement describes the trade-off correctly?

choices.text: Both approaches yield the same chunks when the overlap is set to the same value, so the choice only affects which code library is used
Semantic chunking follows topic shifts and gives self-contained chunks, but it needs embedding calls at ingestion and gives variable sizes that need a cap
Recursive splitting is unsuitable for production because it cuts only at exact character counts and ignores paragraph and sentence boundaries
Semantic chunking is cheaper than recursive splitting because it never calls an embedding model, and it always yields chunks of the same length

stem: A RAG pipeline retrieves 50 candidate passages by vector similarity and passes the top 5 to the LLM. Answer quality improves when a second model re-scores the 50 candidates against the query first. What is the role of that re-ranking step?

choices.text: It replaces the embedding model so that the documents no longer need to be embedded when the search index is built
It expands the user's question into several paraphrases so that the first-stage search covers more of the corpus vocabulary and synonyms
It re-scores a small candidate set with a model that reads the query and each passage together, so the best passages reach the prompt
It compresses each retrieved passage into a shorter summary so that more passages fit into the LLM context window

stem: A developer adds the AI Search reranker to a hybrid query and wants the reranker to also consider a `product_name` metadata column and a `parent_doc_summary` column. Which TWO statements about configuring the reranker are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: `num_results` limits how many candidates the reranker scores, so setting it to 5 means that only five passages are ever re-scored by it
`num_results` is the final number of results returned after reranking and does not change how many candidates are used for reranking
The reranker replaces the query type, so `query_type` must be removed when `reranker` is set
The reranker needs the index to be rebuilt with a separate reranking embedding model before it can be used in a query
Columns for reranking go in `columns_to_rerank`, apart from the `columns` returned, and their order matters because only the first 2,000 characters are read

stem: Two applications use the same AI Search index. One is an internal RAG chatbot where answer quality matters most and users accept a response time of a few seconds. The other is an autocomplete box that must answer within tens of milliseconds at high request volume. How should the reranker be used?

choices.text: Disable it for both, because a reranker lowers retrieval quality whenever hybrid search is already used for the first stage
Enable it for both, because the reranker adds no measurable time to a query and always improves the ordering of results
Enable it for the chatbot, where the added latency buys relevance, and leave it off for the latency-sensitive autocomplete box
Enable it only for the autocomplete box, since short queries have too little text for hybrid search and need a second pass

stem: A team is loading Markdown release notes for a RAG application. The notes use `#` and `##` headings, and each section answers a different question. Which LangChain component is the best fit for splitting them?

choices.text: A `MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter`, which splits on heading levels and keeps the heading text as metadata on each chunk
An `HTMLHeaderTextSplitter`, since Markdown files are rendered as HTML before they are stored
A `CharacterTextSplitter` with a fixed 500-character size, because predictable chunk lengths give consistent embeddings
A `SemanticChunker` run on the raw file, because Markdown syntax cannot be split on its structure

stem: A developer builds a LangChain chain in a Databricks notebook and wants it to call a chat model hosted on a Model Serving endpoint, including a Foundation Model API endpoint. Which integration class from the `databricks-langchain` package should the chain use?

choices.text: `UCFunctionToolkit`, which turns the serving endpoint into a callable chat model for LangChain
`VectorSearchRetrieverTool`, which sends the prompt to the endpoint as a retrieval query
`DatabricksFunctionClient`, which creates the serving endpoint automatically when the chain is invoked
`ChatDatabricks`, which wraps a Databricks serving endpoint as a LangChain chat model

stem: An agent built with LangGraph must search a policy index in AI Search when a user asks a policy question, and the LLM must decide on its own when to call the search. Which approach follows the Databricks recommendation for new Python agents?

choices.text: Wrap the index in a `UCFunctionToolkit` function that returns a fixed list of the most recent documents regardless of the question
Create a `VectorSearchRetrieverTool` with the index name and a tool description saying when to search, and give it to the agent as a tool
Embed the question in application code, call the embedding endpoint directly, and paste the raw vectors into the prompt for the LLM
Fetch all rows of the index's source Delta table into the system prompt before every call, so the LLM reads the full corpus each time

stem: An agent should be able to call an existing Unity Catalog SQL function, `main.hr.lookup_leave_balance`, as a tool. The team already uses LangChain and LangGraph. Which LangChain-compatible tool should they use?

choices.text: `MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter`, which exposes the function name to the agent as a document metadata field
`StrOutputParser`, which executes the named function whenever the LLM responds with plain text
`ChatDatabricks`, passing the function name as the endpoint so that the model runs the function
`UCFunctionToolkit`, created with the function name and a client, whose `.tools` are handed to the agent

stem: A developer tests a LangGraph agent with `UCFunctionToolkit(function_names=["main.sales.top_customers"], client=DatabricksFunctionClient(execution_mode="local"))`. The same code works for a Python function, but `main.sales.top_customers` is a SQL function and the call fails. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Create the client with the default serverless execution mode, which can run SQL functions, and keep the same toolkit
Grant `CREATE FUNCTION` on the schema to the agent, because local mode needs that privilege to run SQL functions
List the function name twice in `function_names` so that the toolkit registers a second copy of the tool for SQL
Wrap the function name in `ChatDatabricks` so that the serving endpoint runs the SQL text for the agent

stem: A workload classifies each of 2 million support tickets into one of five categories with one prompt and one call to a foundation model, with no retrieval, tools or conversation history. A teammate proposes building it with LangChain and LangGraph. What is the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.text: Use LangChain document loaders and a vector retriever, so that the five ticket categories are retrieved before each call
LangGraph is required for any production use of a foundation model, so the job must be rebuilt as an agent graph first
Call the model directly, for example with `ai_query` over the table, since no chain, tool or agent logic is needed
Create a multi-agent supervisor with one agent per category, since each category needs its own separate model

stem: A RAG assistant tells a user that the premium plan includes 24/7 phone support. The retrieved passages, visible in the MLflow trace, mention only email support and do not mention phone support at all. Which diagnosis and check fit this symptom?

choices.text: A retrieval failure; the fix is a larger embedding model, since the phone claim must have come from the index
A formatting problem; the fix is to add a JSON schema to the prompt so that the output is structured
A groundedness failure, an unsupported claim: check it with `RetrievalGroundedness` and restrict the prompt to the context
A latency problem; the fix is to raise the endpoint's concurrency so the model has enough time to read all of the passages

stem: Reviewing traces for a RAG assistant, a developer finds that for the question "How do I reset my router?" the retrieved passages are about mobile-phone plans, and the answer is a fluent but off-topic reply about phone plans. Which statement identifies where the problem is and what to measure?

choices.text: The problem is the system prompt wording, because retrieval can never return off-topic passages for a question
The problem is only how the answer is displayed, because the reply is fluent and the content is therefore correct
Generation is the problem, because a larger LLM would ignore the irrelevant passages and answer from memory
Retrieval is the problem: the context is irrelevant, so measure it (for example with `RetrievalRelevance`) before changing prompt or model

stem: During a manual review of 100 chatbot responses, the team tags issues. Which TWO observed issues are safety problems rather than ordinary quality problems? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A response uses British spelling although the company style guide asks for American spelling in all replies
A response explains in detail how to bypass a building's alarm system when asked for troubleshooting help
A response cites a section number that is one off from the real section
A response answers correctly but uses four paragraphs where one would do
A response repeats a customer's full card number that appeared in a retrieved support ticket

stem: A hiring assistant summarizes resumes. A reviewer suspects that candidates with different given names but identical experience receive different tones of summary. What is the most direct qualitative test of this bias concern?

choices.text: Build paired inputs that differ only in the name and have reviewers or a judge compare tone and content for systematic gaps
Compare only the response length across the candidates, because equal length proves that all candidates were treated equally
Raise the temperature so that the model varies its output enough to hide the differences between groups
Run each response through a spell checker and compare the error counts found across the candidates in each group

stem: Reviewers find that a summarization endpoint's answers often stop in the middle of a sentence, while the retrieved context and the prompt look correct. The responses are all about the same length. What should the developer check first?

choices.text: The retriever's `num_results`, because a higher number of passages removes the end of the generated responses
The generation `max_tokens` setting and the finish reason, since a response cut at a fixed length hit the output limit
The temperature, because a temperature of zero makes the model stop at random places inside its answers
The embedding model's token limit, because truncating chunks at indexing makes the model stop writing early

stem: A support-assistant team wants an automated check that every answer stays polite, avoids promising refunds, and never reveals internal ticket IDs. These are team-specific rules, not generic quality dimensions. Which MLflow evaluation approach fits?

choices.text: A `Guidelines` judge that states each rule in natural language and returns pass or fail for each response
The `RetrievalRelevance` judge, because it checks whether the final answer follows the company rules written by the team
The built-in `Safety` judge alone, because it covers every company-specific policy automatically without any configuration
Manual review of every production response, because LLM judges cannot be given custom criteria of any kind

stem: A knowledge base mixes 100-token FAQ entries with 40-page manuals that have chapter headings. One fixed-size splitter at 500 tokens is used for everything. A per-source evaluation shows that FAQ answers are diluted by neighboring entries and that manual answers are cut across chunks. Which change does this evidence support?

choices.text: Keep the single splitter and add a `doc_type` value to the prompt so that the LLM repairs the cut text itself while answering
Drop the FAQ entries from the index, because short documents cannot be retrieved and the manuals hold the same answers
Split each source type its own way, one chunk per FAQ entry and heading-based chunks for manuals, then re-run the evaluation
Raise the fixed size to 2,000 tokens for every document so that the manuals fit in a few chunks and the FAQ entries stay whole

stem: A team wants to decide between 256-, 512- and 1,024-token chunking. Which evaluation design gives a trustworthy choice?

choices.text: Judge each size on a different set of questions chosen by the engineer who built that particular index for the experiment
Re-index with each size and change the embedding model each time too, since better models produce a better chunk size
Pick the size that produces the fewest chunks, because a smaller index is faster and a faster index is therefore more accurate
Use one fixed set of questions, re-index with each chunk size changing only that variable, and compare retrieval and answer metrics

stem: An evaluation of a RAG assistant on 200 questions shows good retrieval (the right chunk is almost always in the top 5), but answers are often incomplete, and groundedness is high. The missing details sit in the paragraphs directly before and after each retrieved chunk. Which TWO chunking changes does this evidence support? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Switch to much smaller chunks of one or two sentences so that retrieval becomes even more specific
Replace the embedding model with a smaller one, because the retriever is already finding the right chunk
Disable the LLM's use of retrieved context, so that the answers come from its own knowledge
Use parent-child retrieval: keep the small chunks for matching, and return the parent section to the LLM
Increase the chunk size or add overlap so that adjacent paragraphs fall into the same chunk

stem: After raising chunk overlap from 10% to 60%, retrieval precision@5 falls: the top five results often contain nearly identical passages from the same part of one document, and the prompt carries the same sentences repeated. What does the evaluation indicate?

choices.text: Excessive overlap creates near-duplicate chunks that crowd out other results, so reduce overlap or merge adjacent hits
The index is too small, so more documents must be added to remove the repeats
The embedding model has become less accurate, so it must be fine-tuned before the overlap is changed again in any test
The reranker is the cause of the repeats and must be disabled for any index with overlap

stem: A developer compares two chunking strategies. For each question in the evaluation set, the team wants an automatic score of whether the retrieved passages are relevant to the question, without writing expected answers. Which MLflow built-in judge fits?

choices.text: `Correctness`, which compares the response with ground-truth expectations that the team would write for every question
`RetrievalRelevance`, which judges whether the retrieved context is relevant to the request using only inputs and outputs
`Safety`, which scores whether the retrieved context is free from toxic material and answers the question
`RelevanceToQuery`, which scores the retrieved chunks against the question and ignores the generated answer

stem: A knowledge base has two question types: lookups of exact facts (a part number, a deadline) and requests to explain a procedure that spans several paragraphs. A team finds that 200-token chunks win on lookups and lose on procedures, while 800-token chunks do the opposite. Which design best serves both types?

choices.text: Use a single 400-token chunk size and accept the average, since adapting chunk size to the question type is not possible
Use 50-token chunks for both question types and increase the overlap to 90% to compensate for the lost context
Index small chunks for precise lookups and use parent-child or sentence-window expansion so procedures arrive with their section
Keep 800-token chunks for all questions and drop the lookup results from evaluation, since procedures matter more

stem: A user asks, "What is the warranty on the X200 pump?" An AI Search index stores chunks for many products and has a `product` metadata column. The application should narrow retrieval to the product the user named. Which prompt-augmentation step uses the user's input to do this?

choices.text: Retrieve the 50 most recent chunks of any product and let the user choose the right one from them
Extract the product name from the question, with an LLM call or a rule, and apply it as a metadata filter on the index query
Add every product name in the whole catalog to the prompt so that the LLM can guess which one the user means
Increase `num_results` so that the X200 chunks appear somewhere among the many results that are returned

stem: In a chat application, the second turn is "And what about its battery life?" Sent to the retriever as written, the query returns generic battery passages from unrelated devices. What is the appropriate augmentation?

choices.text: Send the entire chat history as the query text, which is guaranteed to improve retrieval for every follow-up question
Ask the user to repeat the product name in every message and reject follow-ups that omit it from the text
Embed only the word "battery" and use a lower similarity threshold, to widen the search across all devices
Rewrite the follow-up into a standalone query using the history (for example "battery life of the X200 pump") and retrieve with it

stem: A banking assistant is told by the application, through request fields, the customer's preferred language and account tier. The answering prompt must use this knowledge on every call. How should the application augment the prompt?

choices.text: Add template variables such as `{language}` and `{account_tier}` to the prompt and fill them from the request fields
Place the language and tier in a model-serving config file so that every user shares the same single setting
Ask the LLM to infer the language and tier from the question text in each turn instead of using request fields
Fine-tune a separate model for each language and tier, so that no information needs to be passed at call time at all

stem: Which TWO steps use the content of a user's question to improve what the retriever returns? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Lower the temperature, so that the same retrieval is repeated for the same user
Increase the LLM's maximum output tokens, so that longer questions can be answered
Classify the question's intent (billing, technical, account) and route it to the matching index, prompt or tool
Store each question in the output Delta table, so that it is available for later audits and for later evaluation
Extract entities and terms such as a product name or error code, and use them as filters or keywords in a hybrid query

stem: A RAG prompt template puts the user's raw question into the instructions: `Use the context to answer. {question} Context: {context}`. Sometimes the model treats parts of the question as instructions and ignores the context. Which prompt-structure change helps most?

choices.text: State instructions first, put context and the question in separate delimited sections, and tell the model to answer only from the context
Move the context before the instructions and remove the instructions entirely, so that the model has to infer the task by itself
Append the user's question a second time at the end so that the model weights it more than the context
Replace the context with a longer, more detailed version of the user's question, so the model has more detail to use

stem: A support assistant built on a foundation model answers correctly, but its replies are long, formal and full of marketing phrases. The brand team wants short, friendly replies of two sentences that sound like a set of approved sample replies. Which change to the prompt moves the output from this baseline to the desired style most reliably?

choices.text: Add a sentence that says "be friendly and brief" to the instructions and raise the temperature so the model sounds less formal and more varied
Paste the whole brand style guide into the prompt and ask the model to follow every rule in it, without showing any sample replies
Ask the model to write the long formal reply first and then to shorten it later in the same answer, keeping both versions visible
Add three to five approved question-and-reply pairs before the new question and state the two-sentence limit

stem: One prompt asks a model to read a customer e-mail, extract the order number, classify the sentiment and draft a reply in the brand voice. In the baseline the reply is good, but the order number is often missing or wrong and the sentiment is sometimes skipped. Which prompt change is the best next step?

choices.text: Add more sentences about the brand voice to the same prompt so that the model has fewer chances to forget the other two parts
Split the work into chained prompts for extraction, sentiment and reply, and pass the extracted fields into the reply prompt
Put the words "this is very important" in capital letters in front of the extraction instruction and repeat that line three times
Paste many more sample e-mails into the same prompt until the model has seen every possible format of an order number

stem: A RAG prompt is `Answer the question. {context} {question}`. In testing, the model sometimes answers from its own memory when the retrieved passages do not contain the answer, and it is hard to tell where the context ends. The team wants answers grounded in the passages only. Which rewrite fixes the baseline best?

choices.text: Put the question first and the passages last, because models only pay attention to the final lines of a prompt and ignore the start
Remove the passages from the prompt and rely on a larger model that has already seen similar documents during its training
Wrap the passages in delimiters, limit the answer to them, and give a fixed "not found in the documents" reply for missing answers
Add the sentence "Do not hallucinate and be accurate" at the end of the prompt and keep the rest of the template exactly as it is

stem: A team has a baseline prompt that scores 70% on a fixed set of 100 evaluation questions. A colleague rewrites the persona, adds four rules, swaps the examples and changes the output layout in one edit. The score rises to 74%, but nobody knows why. What is the best way to continue improving the prompt?

choices.text: Test every new version only on the questions that failed before, because questions that already pass cannot teach the team anything
Judge each version on a handful of favorite questions, since a big set hides the effect of small changes
Change one element at a time, rerun the same fixed evaluation set after each change and keep only the changes that help
Keep the large edit, because any score gain proves that each of the changes was useful

stem: A product manager gives the prompt `Summarize this ticket.` The baseline summaries vary widely in length and focus, and the agents who read them want the customer's problem, the steps already tried and the requested outcome. Which rewritten prompt is the best fix?

choices.text: Summarize the ticket for a support agent in at most 60 words: the problem, the steps tried and the wanted outcome, as three labeled lines.
Summarize this ticket very well and make sure the summary is useful, accurate, complete and short, written the way an expert would write it.
Summarize this ticket in a creative way, and feel free to add anything else you think the reader might find interesting or fun.
Summarize this ticket, then summarize the summary, and repeat that step again and again until the text is as short as it can possibly be.

stem: A public assistant for a bank must only discuss the bank's own products. Users sometimes ask for medical advice or help with homework, and the assistant currently answers. The team wants to prevent these off-topic answers before they reach users. Which guardrail design is most suitable?

choices.text: Lower the temperature to zero, because a deterministic output cannot go off topic when the system prompt describes the bank
Add an input classifier that labels each request in scope or out of scope, and return a fixed polite refusal for out-of-scope requests
Rely on the model's built-in training, since foundation models already refuse everything that is unrelated to the system prompt
Increase the number of retrieved passages so the model has more banking material to talk about instead of unrelated subjects

stem: A children's education app uses a foundation model to write short stories. Rarely, a story contains violent or otherwise unsuitable content, and the team must make sure such text is never shown. Which guardrail placement protects the users?

choices.text: Log every story to a Delta table and have staff review the table once a week to find stories that were unsuitable
Check only the user's prompt for unsafe words before generation, since a clean prompt always produces a clean and suitable story
Tell users in the terms of use that stories may sometimes contain unsuitable content and ask parents to supervise reading
Run a safety classifier on each generated story and replace unsafe results with a safe fallback message or a regeneration

stem: Which TWO guardrails directly reduce the risk of an ungrounded or malformed answer reaching the application that calls a RAG chain? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Raise the maximum output tokens so that the model can write longer answers when a question needs more detail
Increase the embedding dimension of the index so that more information fits in every vector and the passages are richer
Run a groundedness check of the answer against the retrieved passages and return "not found" when claims are unsupported
Move the retriever to a larger cluster so that the retrieved passages arrive at the model faster and with less delay
Validate the model output against the required JSON schema and retry or return an error response when validation fails

stem: Three teams in a company each call the same hosted model from their own applications. Each team wrote its own safety code, and audits found that the rules differ between teams and that one team forgot the check. The platform group wants one consistent set of content rules for every caller. Which approach fits best?

choices.text: Publish a wiki page that describes recommended filtering code and ask each team to copy it into its own application
Move all three applications into one notebook and keep the filtering code in a shared cell that every application runs
Ask the model provider to retrain the model with the company's content rules and release it to all of its customers
Route all three applications through one shared gateway layer in front of the model, where the content checks run on every request and response

stem: A team added an output safety check to a streaming chat application. It checks the full answer only after the model has finished, but users read tokens while they stream, so unsafe text is already visible when the check blocks the answer. What is the best fix that keeps the guardrail?

choices.text: Replace the safety check with a longer system prompt that asks the model politely not to write any unsafe text
Turn off streaming on the safety-critical path, or buffer and check chunks of text before they go to the user interface
Keep streaming as it is and display a warning label next to the answer when the check later reports a failure
Move the safety check so that it runs once before the application starts, at deployment time, instead of on each answer

stem: A retail website adds a chat widget for simple store-hours and return-policy questions. Answers are one or two sentences, traffic is high, and response time must stay well under one second to first token. Which model choice fits the application?

choices.text: A small, fast model, because the tasks are easy and latency and cost per request limit the design
A multimodal video model, because the widget may need to accept new kinds of input in the future
The largest and most capable model available, because answer accuracy is the only property that matters for a website widget
A model with the longest context window, because the widget will receive many questions every hour of the day

stem: A legal team wants a model to answer questions about single contracts that are often about 150,000 tokens long, passing the full contract in the prompt without chunking. Which attribute must the team verify first when comparing candidate models?

choices.text: Whether the embedding dimension of the model is at least 1,024, since long inputs need larger output vectors
Whether the model can return images as output, since contracts contain tables and diagrams that must be redrawn
Whether the model name includes a version number that is higher than the version numbers of the other candidates
Whether the context window can hold the contract, the instructions and the answer together

stem: A company built a prototype on a pay-per-token Foundation Model API. The assistant goes to production with steady, high traffic, and the business needs performance guarantees for the model it uses. Which serving mode should the engineer plan for?

choices.text: Stay on pay-per-token, because it is the only mode that supports production traffic and gives dedicated capacity
Switch to a batch inference pipeline that runs once a night and stores the generated answers in a Unity Catalog table
Move to provisioned throughput, which allocates dedicated capacity with performance guarantees for production
Use AI Functions optimized models, because they are designed for low-latency real-time chat traffic from end users

stem: Which TWO considerations belong in a sound process for choosing the LLM for a new application? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Prefer the model with the shortest name to reduce the size of requests
Check that the model supports the needed input types, such as images in addition to text, and the languages of the users
Choose the model that was released most recently, because newer always means better for a given task
Pick the model with the most parameters, because parameter count predicts quality on every task
Compare candidates on the team's own representative evaluation questions, not on a generic ranking only

stem: A team in a regulated industry picks a hosted model from the catalog listing in `system.ai`. The model name appears in the listing, but when the application calls it from their workspace, the call is rejected as unavailable. What should the engineer check first?

choices.text: Whether the model is available in the workspace region and cross-geo settings, and the user may query the service
Whether the prompt contains more tokens than the answer, since the request is rejected when the ratio is wrong
Whether the request sets a higher temperature, which a model service requires before it can start serving responses
Whether the embedding dimension of the model matches the dimension of the vector index used by the application

stem: A team indexes technical articles in chunks of about 1,200 tokens for retrieval so that each chunk keeps an entire procedure together. They can choose between a hosted embedding model with a 512-token embedding window and a hosted embedding model with an 8,192-token embedding window, both producing 1,024-dimension vectors. Which model should they choose?

choices.text: Either one, because tokens beyond the window are still embedded by an automatic second pass over the text
The 8,192-token model, because the whole 1,200-token chunk then fits into the embedding window
The 512-token model, because both vectors have the same dimension and so the window does not matter
The 512-token model, because a smaller window gives more precise embeddings for any chunk size

stem: What does the embedding window of 512 tokens mean for a text embedding model?

choices.text: The model can read a 512-token question and write a 512-token answer in one chat turn
The model can return at most 512 results from a similarity search over the index
The model creates vectors that have 512 dimensions, one value for each input token

stem: A team has an FAQ corpus in which every entry is about 120 tokens, and user queries are one short sentence. An engineer proposes replacing the current embedding model with one that has a much larger embedding window, expecting better recall. Which assessment is most accurate?

choices.text: It will improve recall in all cases, because larger windows always give more accurate vectors
It will fail, because a model with a much larger window cannot embed short texts such as FAQ entries or one-sentence queries

stem: A RAG application retrieves the top 5 chunks of 1,500 tokens each and puts them into the prompt of a chat model whose context window is 4,096 tokens, together with 500 tokens of instructions and room for an answer of 600 tokens. The embedding model has an 8,192-token embedding window. Requests fail with context length errors. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Retrieve fewer or smaller chunks so instructions, retrieved text and answer fit the chat model's context window
Reduce the embedding window to 4,096 tokens so that the embedding model and the chat model use the same limit
Increase the embedding dimension of the index so that fewer chunks are needed to carry the same information
Switch to an embedding model with an even larger embedding window, so that the retrieved chunks are embedded without limits

stem: Which TWO statements are true when an index built with a 512-token embedding model is replaced with one that uses an 8,192-token embedding model? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The chunk size should still be chosen for good retrieval granularity, not simply raised to the new maximum
The new window makes chunking unnecessary, because whole documents always give the best retrieval
The existing document vectors can stay, and only new documents need the new model
The change affects only the chat model, because embedding models do not produce stored vectors

stem: A team wants an open model for a text-classification step and plans to browse Databricks Marketplace. They want only machine learning models, from a specific provider, that cost nothing. Which approach is correct?

choices.text: Search for the model in Catalog Explorer, because Marketplace listings always exist in the workspace catalog already
Query `system.ai` with SQL, because every Marketplace model is stored in that schema after listing

Search the Marketplace and filter listings by product type (ML model), provider name and cost (free)

stem: A company wants to use an open model in a paid customer-facing product. Two candidates perform equally in tests. The first model card states a license that allows commercial use, the second states that use is restricted to research. What should the team do?

choices.text: Use the second model, because a license in a model card is only a recommendation and not a condition
Use the first model, because its license permits the commercial use that the product needs
Use either one, because licenses apply to the training data only and never to the published model weights
Use the second model and check the license again after the product has launched to customers

stem: After the team gets instant access to a model listing in Databricks Marketplace, where does the model appear in the workspace, and what can the team do with it?

choices.text: Inside the `system.ai` schema, merged with the models that Databricks hosts for Foundation Model APIs
